synthesis.headline: Western block's retreat runs on: a coastal cutoff low soaks and chills the West, southern heat holds firm, and a Maritime cold front fires Southeast storms
synthesis.narrative:
The organizing story is continuity of last week's transition, now clearly past its tipping point. The high-amplitude, blocked backbone Tlaloc tracked all week has broken into a more mobile, three-part arrangement: a broad longwave trough over the Pacific Northwest and western Canada (roughly 570 dam along its axis) with a genuine cutoff low pinched off just offshore of the NorCal/Oregon coast near 583 dam; a still-amplified but transient central ridge over the High Plains (588-592 dam); and a downstream trough digging into the Great Lakes and Northeast. At the surface this shows up as a messy cluster of weak lows over the southern Rockies and High Plains (1007-1010 mb), a cold front draped through the central Plains, and a sharper front pushing across the upper Midwest and Great Lakes with the tightest gradient of the day over the northern Plains. Off the eastern seaboard, a deepening Maritime low (993-994 hPa on the Canadian analysis) is dragging a front southward through the Southeast. The net effect: the interior heat regime is contracting toward the southern tier while cooler, more progressive flow takes over the West and North.

Today's centers of action sit, as they have all week, on the flanks of the retreating ridge rather than in the deep Plains. The offshore western cutoff is the busiest feature: it is driving heavy rain across Utah with urban and burn-scar flood concern, moderate-to-locally-heavy rain into the northern Rockies and northwestern Montana, and a West-wide cool-down of 10-20 degrees below normal with freezing levels dropping toward the Sierra Nevada. The best-organized severe threat is over the Southeast, where a moist tropical airmass and strong heating (MLCAPE ~2000-2500 J/kg) support outflow-dominant, damaging-wind storms from the southern Appalachians into the Savannah River Valley, with the sagging Maritime front the trigger and the cool air behind it breaking the eastern heat into the 70s. A separate, better-sheared threat sits over western/central Montana, where 40-50 kt deep-layer shear favors supercells with large hail. Under the central ridge, the durable signal persists: heat indices of 105-110 degrees and record-warm overnight lows across the midsection. Looking to Canada, a maturing cyclone is set to cross the Prairies and spread strong storms into the northern Plains by Tuesday.

Upstream, the Air Mass RGB anchors the story: a vivid orange-red dry plume arcs from the northern Rockies through the central Plains into the lower Mississippi Valley — low-PV subsidence air on the equatorward flank of the western trough, and the reason the midsection heat holds through capping and midlevel warming rather than because of any modest surface high. Its sharp eastern edge from the central Plains through the Tennessee Valley marks the implied jet corridor, matched by the tightening contours and 60-80 kt flow the DuPage analysis shows across the Great Lakes and Northeast. The central ridge is best described as semi-blocking, not a Rex block: there is no clean high-over-low couplet stacked at one longitude. The decisive question — real regime change or cosmetic flattening — is answered by the ensemble pair, and it points to a genuine transition. At 6-10 days the positive-anomaly signal survives only along the Pacific coast and offshore, with the zero line already retreated to the Intermountain West and contours trending more zonal across the CONUS. By 8-14 days even that coastal ridge gives way to broad negative anomalies extending through western Canada into the Pacific Northwest, the high-latitude ridge collapses into a deep polar low over the Canadian Archipelago, and the only surviving positive anomaly (+6 to +9 dam) has relocated to the Southeast and western Atlantic. That is the ridge shrinking in the west and its core migrating south and east across the two charts — the classic retreat-toward-the-south signature carried through, not a single shortwave passing through a regenerating block. The CPC temperature outlook is geometrically consistent: a 90-100% above-normal bull's-eye clings to the Texas-Oklahoma-New Mexico corner while both coasts lean cool. The falling, solidly negative NAO (7-day mean near -1.0) is directionally consistent with the eastern troughing, but as a weak, lagging summer signal it is a cross-check on the height field, not its basis.
synthesis.climate_context: The ONI table lists a most recent value of -0.60 — nominally still on the cold side — but with a forecast trajectory toward warming and El Niño development, and the tropical field is already behaving in El Niño-leaning fashion: a hyperactive East Pacific carrying Hurricane Marie west of southern Baja (well-organized with curved banding on the full-disk RGB), Hurricane Lowell and Tropical Storm Karina near Hawaii, and a 60%-in-seven-days disturbance offshore southwestern Mexico, set against a completely suppressed Atlantic where NHC expects no development for seven days at what is climatologically the season's peak. The North American Monsoon remains active, feeding the Utah/Southwest heavy-rain and flood threat and the fragmented afternoon convection over Mexico on the RGB. Severe weather continues to express itself in its expected late-summer mode — ridge-periphery and frontal storms across the West, northern Plains, and Southeast rather than deep-Plains outbreaks — while the most durable domestic signal remains the central-U.S. heat, now consolidating over the south-central Plains as the western ridge retreats southward.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions and none issued in the past six hours. Watch the western/central Montana supercell corridor for large hail as the primary threat and the southern Appalachians into the Savannah River Valley for damaging winds from outflow-dominant, high-PW storms. Localized flash-flood risk runs across Utah on the western upper low, including urban and burn-scar sensitivity, with a slight excessive-rainfall risk into northwestern Montana. In Canada, the strongest domestic surface winds sit along the Prairie gradient beneath the interior high, and a maturing cyclone crossing the Canadian Prairie is expected to spread strong storms into the northern Plains by Tuesday. Out West, freezing levels dropping toward the Sierra Nevada are notable this early in September.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 0900Z 6 September 2026 WPC surface analysis shows a complex multi-center pattern across the contiguous US. The most prominent low pressure area sits across the southern Rockies and adjacent High Plains, with several centers reading near 1007-1010 mb, connected by a trailing cold front that extends southward through the central plains and a stationary or slow-moving frontal segment across the southern tier; a separate low near the Texas-New Mexico border reads around 1007-1008 mb and anchors what appears to be an occluded or quasi-stationary boundary. A well-defined cold front pushes across the upper Midwest and Great Lakes, with the sharp wind-shift symbols and tightly spaced isobars in the northern plains suggesting the steepest gradient on the chart there, and this front is the primary lifting mechanism for the northern tier. A broad high pressure ridge dominates the eastern seaboard with centers near 1021-1022 mb over the Great Lakes and mid-Atlantic, and a separate 1022 mb high sits over the Canadian maritimes, together producing southerly to southeasterly flow feeding Gulf moisture northward through the Mississippi Valley and into the frontal zones across the central plains, where dewpoints in the mid-60s to low-70s F are visible. The western US shows a weak pressure gradient overall with slack flow and a diffuse low off the California coast near 1006 mb, consistent with subsidence and onshore marine layer flow but no organized lifting mechanism apparent at the surface.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Sunday 06 September 2026 shows a broad high pressure ridge across much of interior Canada, with centers near 1027 hPa over what appears to be the central Canadian Prairies and another around 1025-1026 hPa positioned over the central United States, together establishing a large anticyclonic dome that likely suppresses precipitation from the northern Plains northward through Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Along the Pacific facade, a low near 995 hPa sits over the Gulf of Alaska region with an associated frontal system trailing southeastward, and the implied onshore pressure gradient would focus lift and moisture transport into coastal British Columbia. Across the eastern side of the domain, a low labeled near 993-994 hPa appears positioned over the Atlantic seaboard or adjacent waters east of the Maritime provinces, with frontal boundaries curling westward that could bring unsettled conditions to Atlantic Canada and possibly Quebec. In the high Arctic portion of the chart, upper frame lows of 989-999 hPa are present but these sit over the Arctic Ocean and Archipelago well north of the provinces and carry no direct implication for Canadian populated areas. Tropical Storm Karina is annotated at 21.8N 143.7W and Hurricane Marie at 22.3N 121.0W, both far out in the western Pacific and eastern Pacific respectively, outside the area of Canadian weather concern on this chart.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 1200 UTC 6 September 2026, the 500 mb pattern shows a broad longwave trough across the Pacific Northwest and western Canada, with heights near 570 dam along the trough axis, while a pronounced ridge axis extends from the central Rockies northward into the northern Plains, with heights reaching approximately 588-592 dam over the central High Plains where two H centers are plotted. The ridge is moderately amplified and the overall wavelength is long, giving the pattern a relatively slow, retrogressive character rather than a progressive one. A closed low is marked with an L off the Pacific Northwest coast near the northern California-Oregon offshore zone, with the lowest contour appearing to close around 583 dam, indicating it is genuinely cut off from the main westerlies and will tend to pivot rather than translate rapidly downstream. Downstream across the eastern United States, height contours tighten toward the Northeast, consistent with an implied jet corridor orienting roughly west-southwest to east-northeast across the Great Lakes and mid-Atlantic, with wind barbs in that corridor suggesting speeds on the order of 60-80 knots. The overall pattern is one of a quasi-stationary amplified western ridge flanked by the offshore cutoff low to the northwest and a downstream trough digging into the Great Lakes-Northeast region, with the central ridge acting as a semi-blocking feature rather than a textbook Rex block, since there is no clear high-over-low meridional couplet at a single longitude.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: The most striking feature is a broad, vivid orange-red dry airmass signature arcing across the northwestern quadrant of the domain, from the northern Rockies and northern Plains southeastward through the central Plains and into the lower Mississippi Valley, consistent with deep dry air on the equatorward and downstream flank of an upper trough centered off the northern edge of the image. The sharpest color boundary along the eastern edge of this orange swath, running roughly from the central Plains through the Tennessee Valley, marks the likely jet corridor implied by the strong airmass contrast there. South and east of that boundary, a broad green moist tropical airmass fills the Gulf Coast states, the Southeast, and extends well offshore into the Atlantic, with scattered white high-cloud clusters over the Gulf Coast, peninsular Florida, and the western Atlantic indicating organized deep convection embedded in this moist regime. A separate, more compact tongue of orange-red dry air is visible over the northern Great Lakes and into the Northeast, which on the cyclonic flank of any ridge or trough feature there warrants attention as a possible stratospheric intrusion, though its somewhat diffuse character makes that interpretation uncertain. Over Mexico, fragmented deep convective clusters appear in white against the green moist background, likely associated with diurnally driven afternoon convection.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: At 1310 UTC 6 September 2026, the airmass RGB shows a well-organized tropical cyclone off the Pacific coast of Mexico's Baja California peninsula, exhibiting a clear curved banding structure in white high cloud tops against the surrounding orange-red dry upper-tropospheric air, indicating a system already in a relatively dry environment on its northern and western flanks. A broad swath of green moisture extends from the Caribbean westward across Central America and southern Mexico, with scattered clusters of bright white convective tops embedded along what appears to be the ITCZ corridor across the eastern Pacific. Across Canada and the northern tier of the domain, a sharp boundary separates blue-purple cold dry upper-level air over the high latitudes from greener airmasses to the south, with the implied polar jet axis running roughly from the northwestern Canadian interior toward the Great Lakes region and curving into the North Atlantic. A compact, swirling feature is visible in the lower left of the disk near the southeastern Pacific, consistent with a Southern Hemisphere extratropical system. Southern South America displays a stark orange-red region over Patagonia and the adjacent South Atlantic, consistent with dry descending air on the eastern side of the Andes, with a separate circulation evident south of the continent embedded in the Southern Ocean westerlies.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a broad above-normal signal centered on Texas and the surrounding southern plains, where the darkest shading indicates a 90-100% probability of above-normal temperatures in a compact core straddling roughly the Texas-Oklahoma-New Mexico border region; this grades outward through 80-90% and 70-80% probabilities across most of the south-central and southeastern United States, and the above-normal signal extends at lower confidence, 40-60%, well into the central and northern plains and upper Midwest. The Pacific Northwest coast and coastal Oregon are shaded for below-normal temperatures at 33-40% probability, while New England and the immediate mid-Atlantic coast carry a similar leaning-below signal, though both are at the weakest confidence tier and represent a narrow fringe compared to the expansive warmth dominating the rest of the country. Alaska and Hawaii are both favored for above normal, consistent with a broadly amplified warm pattern across much of North America. The tight, high-confidence warm bull's-eye over the south-central plains, paired with cooler signals at both coasts, is geometrically consistent with a persistent amplified ridge over the interior at upper levels, implying the model guidance through this period does not resolve a significant pattern break but rather supports continuation of a heat-retaining anticyclonic regime over the southern and central United States. The below-normal leaning confined to the Pacific coast and the Northeast suggests those areas may sit on the flanks of that implied ridge rather than under a distinct separate trough of high confidence.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast, valid 11-15 September 2026, with green solid contours for heights at 60 m intervals and dashed contours for anomalies.

The dominant height anomaly feature is a strong positive center over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and adjacent waters, with anomaly contours reaching +90 dam — this almost certainly represents a value of +9 dam (90 m), consistent with the scale for 500 mb anomalies, and I flag the label ambiguity rather than asserting the four-digit reading. A secondary positive anomaly of similar magnitude appears along the Pacific coast of the contiguous western United States and into the eastern Pacific, while broad negative anomalies of roughly -30 dam (read as -3 dam) are depicted over the central and eastern Pacific, the northeastern U.S. and Atlantic seaboard, and across portions of the North Pacific.

The 500 mb height ridge axis, inferred from the packing and curvature of the green contours, runs roughly meridionally along or just west of the British Columbia and Pacific Northwest coast, with heights near 576-582 dam at mid-latitudes there. A broad trough axis is implied across the north-central Pacific. The zero-anomaly line appears to cross into the western interior of North America — roughly the Intermountain West — meaning positive anomalies do not extend deeply into the continental interior, and the ridge is relatively confined to the coast and offshore; the pattern is consistent with a weakening or retreating western ridge rather than a building or amplifying one, and the tightly packed, more zonally oriented height contours across the mid-latitudes of the CONUS suggest a trend toward more zonal flow over the period.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly prognostic valid 13–19 September 2026, made 5 September 2026, so it is indeed an 8–14 day product as described. The green contours show 500 mb heights in dam at 60 dam intervals, with the labeled values running from roughly 534 dam near a closed low center over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago up through 588 dam or so across the southern tier of the contiguous United States; the dashed contours in red and blue are the height anomalies, also at 60-unit intervals — given the scale these are almost certainly in meters, so the labeled values of roughly +90 m, +30 m, 0, −30 m, −60 m, and −90 m correspond to anomalies of about +9, +3, 0, −3, −6, and −9 dam. The dominant feature is a deep negative anomaly center (around −6 dam, near the −60 contour) positioned over the Canadian Arctic, collocated with the closed height low near 534 dam over the Archipelago, with the negative anomaly field extending broadly southward through western Canada into the Pacific Northwest. Over western Canada, the northern Rockies, and the northern Plains the anomaly contours show near-zero to weakly negative departures, indicating no meaningful positive anomaly ridge in that region; the ridge axis, identified by the most poleward extent of the height contours, appears to be positioned well to the west over the eastern Pacific and then curves sharply into the Canadian Arctic, placing any ridge core offshore rather than over the northern Rockies or Plains. A broad positive anomaly region of roughly +6 to +9 dam (near the +60 and +90 dashed contours) is centered over the southeastern United States and western Atlantic, consistent with a ridge core retreated toward the southern Plains and Gulf Coast rather than anchored over the northern interior.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Cool air from a deepening Maritime low brings scattered strong to severe thunderstorms across the Southeast today into tonight, with slight risk highlighted. Behind the front, heat breaks in the East with highs only mid-70s to low-80s and lows dropping to 40s-50s across New England. Western pattern features a deep upper-level low driving heavy rain across Utah today with urban/burn scar flooding concerns. Consolidating low pressure over northern High Plains yields moderate to locally heavy rain across northern Rockies Labor Day, with slight risk of excessive rainfall in northwestern Montana. Strong thunderstorms expected from northern Plains spreading eastward Tuesday as maturing cyclone moves across Canadian Prairie. Heat persists across midsection with heat indices 105-110 degrees and record warm overnight temperatures widespread through the weekend. West sees temperatures 10-20 degrees below normal with freezing elevations as far south as Sierra Nevada.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
Slight risk issued for severe thunderstorms across southern Appalachians into Savannah River Valley and western/central Montana, with additional isolated severe threat across Interior West, northern/central High Plains, and eastern Dakotas into Ozark Plateau and Gulf Coast.

Southeast: Moist airmass with strong afternoon heating (low-mid 90s) will generate MLCAPE around 2000-2500 J/kg. Weak shear favors outflow-dominant storms; damaging wind gusts likely, isolated hail possible.

Montana: Deep-layer shear of 40-50 kt supports supercells with large hail as primary threat.

Remaining areas: Weak shear and modest forcing limit organization, though isolated damaging winds or hail possible from pulse development and storm interactions along boundaries and terrain-induced convergence zones.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No active mesoscale convective threat is currently being monitored by SPC. No mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next seven days.

East Pacific: Three active systems under NHC advisories—Hurricane Lowell south-southwest of Hawaii, Tropical Storm Karina east-northeast of Hawaii, and Hurricane Marie west of Baja California's southern tip. A disorganized trough several hundred miles south-southwest of southwestern Mexico may gradually develop into a tropical depression mid-to-late week while moving west-northwestward at 10-15 mph. Formation probability: 10 percent through 48 hours, 60 percent through seven days.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ENSO remains in cold phase (La Niña) with most recent ONI reading at -0.60. Anomalies are gradually warming through early 2026. Forecasts show transition to neutral conditions by late winter, followed by shift toward El Niño by mid-year 2026. Most pronounced warmth arrives in summer 2026 with anomalies reaching 1.80, indicating moderate-to-strong El Niño development likely by boreal summer.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA remains modestly negative (-0.34, 7-day mean -0.58) with little directional shift, supporting weak troughing in the East and ridging in the West. AO bounced to +0.53 after dipping negative earlier this week; the 7-day mean near zero shows recent volatility. NAO has fallen notably to -0.66 (7-day mean -1.01, down 0.49), favoring a negative phase that could hinder eastward escape of Atlantic features. Given summer's weak teleconnection signal, these indices provide directional context rather than strong mechanistic guidance.
